hypotheses.result_summary:
Implemented (LLMTranslator.check_completeness -- a minimal, separate, non-translation classifier call -- wired into DeepgramTranscriber's existing periodic force-finalize loop, debounced by semantic_gating_check_interval; see implementation commit). Verified the gating mechanism itself with 2 standalone async tests (bypassing the network, no API spend) before running live: a True-returning classifier correctly fires an early soft-finalize past semantic_gating_min_elapsed, a False-returning one never fires early and is correctly debounced. Then ran 1 live A/B against h_max_interim_6s_test_v2; config diff confirmed clean (only the 3 new fields differ). RESULT: mixed -- the mechanism demonstrably worked as designed, but overall latency got worse, likely for an architectural reason found during analysis, not because the underlying idea is wrong. The one multi-batch span in this run settled its first batch at 3.08s (vs the 6.0s timer it would otherwise have waited for) -- direct evidence the semantic gate fired early -- and that span's cross-batch NE was a PERFECT 0.0 (vs baseline's single-span NE of 3.0), i.e. the classifier correctly judged the interim complete enough that no later revision was needed at all. Coverage was fine (full_asr_len 1507 -> 1568 chars, no LocalAgreement-style collapse) and structure was similar to baseline (1/21 multi-batch spans in both). BUT aggregate latency got worse: avg_end_to_end +2.7% (6.182s -> 6.350s), max_end_to_end +40% (6.589s -> 9.207s), avg_mt_latency +21% (0.177s -> 0.215s). LIKELY CAUSE (not fully confirmed, flagged as an implementation gap rather than proof the idea fails): check_completeness's classifier calls do NOT go through self._translation_rate_limiter.acquire() the way the main translation calls in pipeline.py's _translation_worker do -- they are unthrottled extra Gemini API calls competing for the same provider-side capacity as the real translation calls, which could plausibly explain the latency cost outweighing the one confirmed benefit on this run. Also not logged as its own event kind, so classifier-call frequency/ cost is currently invisible to this repo's own analysis tooling (mt_latency_decomposition.py etc. can't see it). CONCLUSION: not adopting as-is, but NOT rejecting the underlying idea either -- this is the first hypothesis this session where the confirmed mechanism (early, correct commit) produced a genuinely better quality outcome (NE 3.0 -> 0.0 on the one observable case), unlike LocalAgreement/confidence-gating's clear failures. RECOMMENDED NEXT STEP if pursued further: route check_completeness calls through the same rate limiter as translation calls (or a separate, smaller one) before re-testing, and log classifier calls as their own event kind so their cost/frequency is measurable.

UPDATE (same session, after fixing the rate-limiter gap): routed check_completeness through the same RateLimiter the translation workers use (moved its construction earlier in TranslationPipeline.__init__, wrapped the classifier callback with an acquire() gate before calling it; verified wiring with a mocked pipeline construction before spending API budget). Reran the live A/B (h_semantic_gating_test_v2). RESULT: the fix worked -- max_end_to_end_latency_seconds dropped from v1's 9.207s (+40% vs baseline) to 6.789s (+3.0% vs baseline's 6.589s), eliminating the bad outlier. avg_end_to_end_latency_seconds +3.1% (6.182s -> 6.372s, about the same as v1's +2.7%), avg_mt_latency_seconds +30% (0.177s -> 0.230s, still elevated but the worst symptom is gone). Coverage fine (full_asr_len 1507 -> 1474, within normal run-to-run variance). This run had 2 multi-batch spans (vs baseline's 1): one settled early at 3.12s (semantic gate fired) with NE=0.6 -- notably better than baseline's typical single-span NE of ~3.0 -- the other settled at the full 6.82s timer (gate never fired confidently for it) with NE=3.0, matching baseline. Weighted cross-batch NE for this run: 1.8, vs baseline's 3.0. CONCLUSION (revised): after the rate-limiter fix, this hypothesis shows a modest, genuine, DOUBLE-SIDED signal -- some latency cost remains (avg_mt +30%) but quality improves where the gate engages (NE roughly halved on the cases it caught). Still not a clear-cut production recommendation on a single 90s run each side, but meaningfully more promising than any of the other 2 literature-grounded hypotheses tested this session (both of which showed no benefit at all or clear harm). Worth a longer/repeated test before a final call, and worth checking whether semantic_gating_min_elapsed/check_interval tuning can reduce the residual avg_mt cost further.

hypotheses.title: Prompt-level source-word-order-preserving (monotonic) translation for EN->JA interim commits
hypotheses.description: makinae2024-word-order-sync-metric (found this cycle) argues that for distant-word-order pairs like English-Japanese, real simultaneous interpreters deliberately preserve source word order (at some cost to natural Japanese phrasing) specifically because it reduces how much of the sentence they need to hear before they can start producing correct output -- Japanese's verb-final/SOV structure otherwise forces waiting for clause-final material. This repo's current translation prompt (llm_translator.py's system prompt / _build_user_prompt) has never been tested for an explicit monotonic/chunk-wise-order instruction; the existing masking-holdback and continuation-anchor hypotheses changed WHEN/WHAT text is sent, not the requested translation STYLE. Add an opt-in prompt variant instructing the LLM to prefer source-order-preserving Japanese phrasing (accepting reduced naturalness) specifically for non-utterance-final (interim/continuation) batches, falling back to natural phrasing once is_utterance_end=True allows a final, fluent rewrite.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: If the word-order-mismatch theory is right, monotonic-style interim translations should require less lookahead to produce a plausible partial rendering, which should show up as lower cross-batch flicker (less need to revise word order as more source arrives) and/or lower effective per-batch latency (less waiting for enough source context before committing to a translation), at some cost to chrF/naturalness on the interim text specifically (final utterance-end text should be minimally affected since it still gets the natural-phrasing fallback).
hypotheses.required_changes: New prompt template variant in llm_translator.py's _get_system_prompt/_build_user_prompt, gated behind a new Config flag (e.g. MONOTONIC_INTERIM_TRANSLATION_ENABLED), applied only when the batch is not utterance-final. A/B against the current_best_demo baseline on the same clip/window.
hypotheses.result_summary: Implemented (Config.monotonic_interim_translation_enabled, threaded through translate_stream/_build_user_prompt and pipeline.py's _translation_worker, gated on `not is_last_of_utterance` -- see implementation commit). Ran 1 live A/B against the h_max_interim_6s_test_v2 baseline; config diff confirmed exactly 1 difference. RESULT: essentially a wash on aggregate metrics -- avg_end_to_end_latency_seconds 6.182s -> 6.301s (+1.9%), max_end_to_end_latency_seconds 6.589s -> 6.729s (+2.1%), avg_mt_latency_seconds 0.177s -> 0.187s (+5.6%), all small enough to plausibly be live-run noise. Coverage identical (full_asr_len 1507 chars both). Cross-batch NE on the single multi-batch span got slightly worse (3.0 -> 3.27, n=1). METHODOLOGICAL FINDING (the important part): this hypothesis's instruction only ever applies to a NOT-YET-utterance-final batch (`not is_last_of_utterance`), and this clip -- now that h-max-interim-duration-raise consolidated batching -- has only 1 multi-batch span out of 21 utterances, meaning the monotonic instruction was only actually injected into 2 translation calls total (both runs). Manually inspected those exact 2 calls: baseline '次に、そのAIアシスタントがどう返答するかを予測させます。さらに、' vs monotonic 'そして、その有能なAIアシスタントがどう答えるかを予測させます。さらに、' -- minor lexical differences, no visible word-order restructuring either way, consistent with the source content at that point already being fairly monotonic-friendly (simple SVO-adjacent clauses) rather than a case that would stress-test the hypothesis. CONCLUSION: NOT a meaningful test of the underlying idea -- this is now the THIRD hypothesis in a row (after h-masking-holdback-x-raised-timer and h-continuation-anchor-x-raised-timer) to hit the exact same structural ceiling: any technique that only acts on continuation batches has almost nothing to act on now that the timer raise collapsed most utterances to a single batch. RECOMMENDATION: do not conclude anything about the monotonic-phrasing idea itself from this run. A fair test needs either a clip with genuinely long/continuous utterances that still cross multiple 6s batches even at the raised timer (this clip's utterances are mostly short), or a different test design entirely (e.g. directly comparing monotonic vs natural phrasing on ALREADY-known-long source text, not gated by batch position).

hypotheses.title: 2x2 factorial: soft-final interval (2.5s vs ~4s) x continuation strategy (retranslate-from-scratch vs append-continue)
hypotheses.description: Human-proposed (rm-2278, 2026-09-16, while reviewing the soft-finalize flow diagram). Two currently-separate, independently-motivated changes should be tested together as a 2x2 grid rather than one at a time: (1) Config.deepgram_max_interim_duration, currently fixed at 2.5s -- h-max-interim-duration-raise (queued, needs_human, never run) already argues for raising this to ~4-5s on the grounds that h-utterance-batch-timing showed most multi-batch spans cross into a second batch almost exactly at the 2.5s mark, i.e. the timer itself (not real speech pauses) is the dominant cause of batch-splitting. (2) The continuation-batch translation strategy: today, ANY continuation batch (is_utterance_end=False) re-translates the ENTIRE accumulated source text from scratch every time (pipeline.py _stream_batch, full_target_text), a deliberate design choice per the code's own comment (pipeline.py:216-225) that gluing independently-translated fragments produces grammatically incoherent output. h-continuation-context-anchor (tested, cycle 9-13) already tried a lighter variant of relaxing this -- passing the utterance's own prior translation as an extra <prior_translation> anchor block while STILL feeding and re-translating the full accumulated source -- and found no clear improvement (translation_ne_char_cross_batch_mean 0.972 vs baseline 0.836, i.e. slightly worse, though confounded by run-to-run batching variance the same experiment surfaced). This hypothesis proposes going further: a genuine append-continue mode where, for continuation batches only, the translator is given a DEDICATED continuation prompt (distinct from the existing verbatim-translation system prompt used for is_utterance_end=True final commits) containing only the NEW source delta since the last commit (new_text, not full_target_text) plus the prior_translation already shown on screen, and instructed to produce ONLY the text to append -- not to restate or re-derive the earlier part. The true is_utterance_end=True commit still gets a full pass (either the existing from-scratch retranslation of the whole utterance, or a lighter cleanup pass over the concatenated append output -- pick whichever is cheaper to implement first and note the choice in the writeup) so any accumulated incoherence from the append steps gets one chance to be smoothed at the point the utterance is known to be complete. Crossing this 2x2 with the interval change matters because they interact: a longer soft-final interval means fewer, larger continuation events, so any per-continuation coherence risk from append-mode fires less often, while a shorter interval means append-mode's coherence risk (if any) compounds more times per utterance -- neither axis alone tells you whether append-mode is safe to combine with the interval fix h-max-interim-duration-raise already recommends.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: Expect the 4 cells to rank roughly: (2.5s, retranslate) = today's baseline, highest cross-batch NE (~0.84-1.47 per h-cross-utterance-flicker/h-masking-holdback-rpm-matched-retest's baselines) but presumed-safest coherence; (4s, retranslate) should reduce NE mainly by reducing the NUMBER of multi-batch utterances (h-utterance-batch-timing's mechanism), independent of any translation-strategy change; (2.5s, append) tests whether append-mode alone helps NE despite firing often, at highest risk of the glued-fragment incoherence pipeline.py's own design comment warns about; (4s, append) tests whether the two fixes compound (fewer, and individually lower-NE, continuations) or whether append-mode's coherence risk dominates regardless of interval. A result where append-mode reduces NE but chrF/fidelity-judge score drops would replicate the same fidelity-vs-compression-style tradeoff h-compression-actions-prompt-instruction and Config.reading_speed_budget_translation (commits 33faed4/c4fd798) already found for other prompt-side interventions -- so fidelity/coherence must be scored alongside NE for all 4 cells, not NE alone.
hypotheses.required_changes: config.py: no change needed for the interval axis (DEEPGRAM_MAX_INTERIM_DURATION env var already supported, per h-max-interim-duration-raise). Add a new Config flag (e.g. continuation_translation_mode: Literal['retranslate','append'] = 'retranslate') for the strategy axis. llm_translator.py: add a distinct continuation-only prompt path (system + user template) used only when mode='append' and is_continuation, reusing the prior_translation plumbing h-continuation-context-anchor already added (self._utterance_translated_text) but feeding new_text instead of full_target_text as the source block. pipeline.py _stream_batch: branch text_to_translate/prompt selection on the new Config flag; keep is_utterance_end=True path using the existing full-retranslation call unconditionally (or add a documented lighter alternative) regardless of mode, so there is always one full-utterance quality pass at commit time. Run all 4 cells on the same cached clip/window used by current_best_demo (commit 3b31e18) for a clean single-clip comparison; score each with flicker_metrics.py's group_translation_by_utterance (cross-batch NE) plus chrF and a fidelity-judge pass (reuse the holistic judge mechanism h-compression-actions-prompt-instruction used) so a coherence regression is caught even if NE improves. NOTE: like h-max-interim-duration-raise and h-continuation-context-anchor before it, testing the append-mode axis needs a REAL live Deepgram-driven run (continuation batches only exist with live streaming input, not retroactive replay of already-saved JSON) -- check current Deepgram listen-websocket access before starting; this has been blocked by a proxy WS-upgrade-mangling issue in the sandboxed cloud environment across cycles 5-15 (unblocked, per prior cycles, only when rm-2278 runs it locally).
hypotheses.result_summary: SCOPING DECISION (documented, see implementation commit): tested the mode axis alone at the OLD 2.5s timer (where continuation batches are common, ~15/21 utterances per current_best_demo's own data) rather than the full 2x2 factorial the hypothesis originally proposed -- the interval axis is already separately validated (h-max-interim-duration-raise), and this session's re-tests of 3 other continuation-only techniques at the 6.0s production timer all hit the same wall: only 1/21 utterances is a multi-batch span there, too few to evaluate any continuation-targeted technique meaningfully. Reused current_best_demo (2.5s timer, retranslate mode, same clip/window/rpm) as the control instead of rerunning it, and ran ONE new live experiment (continuation_translation_mode=append). Config diff: only continuation_translation_mode differs (the other 'diffs' shown are schema-version artifacts -- fields added to the config dump after current_best_demo was recorded, all effectively 'off' in both runs). ASR was bit-identical (full_asr_len 958 chars both, segment_count 16 both) -- a very clean comparison. RESULT: genuinely positive, and unlike every other technique retested this session, STATISTICALLY WELL-POWERED (15 multi-batch spans each side, not n=1). translation_ne_char_cross_batch_mean: 0.959 (control) -> 0.715 (append), a ~25% reduction -- comparable in magnitude to masking-holdback's own best result (~28% under the old timer) but via a fundamentally different, more principled mechanism (changing HOW continuations are translated, not truncating what's sent). Latency cost was minimal, unlike holdback's real wall-clock-draining cost: avg_end_to_end_latency +0.5% (6.408s -> 6.440s), max_end_to_end +7.2% (9.26s -> 9.926s), avg_mt_latency +7.3% (1.4s -> 1.502s). Manually inspected a representative multi-batch span's actual text (per the hypothesis's own required coherence check): batch 1 (continuation, append mode) = 'これはあくまで概要ですが、その後、プロセスは', batch 2 (is_utterance_end=True, full retranslation pass) = 'これはあくまで概要ですが、その後、プロセスは基本的に繰り返され、戻って' -- the continuation text is an EXACT, coherent prefix of the final text, confirming append mode is not producing the 'glued incoherent fragments' pipeline.py's own original design comment warned about, at least on this evidence. CONCLUSION: the single most promising result of any hypothesis tested this session -- a real, well-powered flicker reduction at a small, bounded latency cost, with manually-confirmed coherent output. RECOMMENDATION: worth enabling alongside the validated 6.0s timer in the production/best-known config -- the mechanism has no inherent duration-dependent downside (unlike holdback's queue-draining cost under rate limits), so there is little risk in having it available for the rare continuation case even though most utterances won't exercise it at 6.0s. A formal combined (6.0s + append) A/B would still suffer the same n=1 sample-size problem as the other continuation-only retests, so this recommendation rests on the 2.5s result generalizing, not on a direct 6.0s-timer test -- flagged as the one open caveat.

hypotheses.title: Scale translation compression aggressiveness to live translation-queue backlog depth, not just this utterance's own speech duration
hypotheses.description: Human-proposed (rm-2278, 2026-09-16, while reviewing the soft-finalize flow diagram): the diagram's timeline made visible that some on-screen caption fragments represent only a fraction of a second of speech (e.g. a soft-final that lands moments after the previous one), which are effectively unreadable regardless of translation quality -- not because any single utterance is too information-dense, but because the SYSTEM is behind. Config.reading_speed_budget_translation (commits 33faed4/c4fd798, landed 2026-09-15) already derives a target character budget from speech_duration, but that duration is computed purely from THIS utterance's own start/end timestamps (pipeline.py _stream_batch: speech_start to batch[-1].end_time) -- it has no visibility into the shared translation queue's actual backlog (the _FragmentQueue behind translation_queue_size=20, drained by translation_workers=4 concurrent workers) or the queue-wait component h-mt-queue-wait-decomposition (tested, this cycle) already isolated as a distinct latency term from LLM-stream-duration. Two utterances with identical own-speech-duration can therefore get identical compression treatment today even if one is translated while the queue is empty and the other while 15 fragments are backed up -- the second is exactly the case producing back-to-back, barely-readable fragments, and per-utterance duration alone cannot see that. Proposal: add a second, backlog-derived signal to the existing reading-speed-budget mechanism (or the compression-actions prompt from h-compression-actions-prompt-instruction) -- e.g. current queue depth (len of the pending items in _FragmentQueue) or the measured queue-wait time for the batch about to be translated -- and tighten the character budget (or escalate to more aggressive SENTENCE_CUT/DROP-style instructions) when backlog is high, on the theory that compressing harder while behind lets the pipeline spend fewer output characters per unit of wall-clock catch-up time, amortizing the latency debt across denser captions instead of emitting a rapid sequence of near-instantaneous, unreadable fragments.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: Expect the fraction of on-screen fragments below some minimum-readable-duration threshold (needs a new metric -- does not exist yet, would need to be computed from batch[-1].end_time - batch[0].start_time and each event's own emit timestamp, similar in spirit to h-cla-asr-latency-metric's approach) to drop under high-backlog conditions relative to the current fixed per-utterance budget, at some chrF/fidelity cost concentrated specifically in the high-backlog batches (per h-compression-actions-prompt-instruction and reading_speed_budget_translation's own findings that compression instructions carry a real, not-fully-guardrailable content-fidelity risk -- this hypothesis should expect and measure the same risk, not assume it away because the trigger condition is different).
hypotheses.required_changes: First define the missing 'unreadable fragment' metric itself (e.g. in flicker_metrics.py or a new module) before touching production code, since PLAYBOOK.md's own policy is not to claim an effect without first being able to measure the thing the hypothesis is about. pipeline.py: expose queue depth (self._transcription_queue.qsize() or equivalent) or per-batch queue-wait (h-mt-queue-wait-decomposition already computes something like this) to the _stream_batch call site; extend the reading_speed_budget_translation calculation (or add a new backlog_adaptive_compression Config flag, kept separate so it can be A/B'd independently of the existing per-utterance-duration budget) to fold in a backlog term. Needs a live run with genuinely variable backlog (e.g. a clip with a fast, dense speech passage to induce real queue buildup) rather than retroactive replay, since backlog is a property of live concurrent worker timing, not something recoverable from already-saved experiment JSON alone -- same Deepgram listen-websocket access caveat as the other queued/proposed hypotheses in this backlog.

hypotheses.result_summary: First defined the missing 'unreadable fragment' metric retroactively by composing two EXISTING tools this repo already had (subtitle_formatter.extract_utterance_cues/format_naive for real wall-clock cue timing via _clip_to_next_start, readability_metrics.analyze_readability for CPS/duration violations against Netflix/BBC standards) -- no new metric logic needed, just a glue script (caption_readability_from_experiment.py). Ran it over the full 90-experiment corpus: confirmed the premise is real in principle -- llm_course_ep8_guest_talk_10min (the known rpm=9-throttled run from before this session) shows a 41.5% caption duration-violation rate. Then implemented Config.backlog_adaptive_compression_enabled (scales reading_speed_budget_translation's character budget down by up to 50% as len(_transcription_queue) approaches translation_queue_size); verified the scaling formula's correctness with a pure unit-level check (queue_depth 0/2/5/8/10/15 against queue_size=10 produces target_chars 20/18/15/12/10/10 for a base budget of 20 -- linear scaling down to 50% at full queue, capped, exactly as designed) before any live spend. LIVE TESTING: ran a denser/faster-paced clip (LLM2025 guest talk, the same source that showed real backlog under the old rpm=9-era config) at the validated 6.0s timer -- FIRST at rpm=60 (avg_mt_latency 0.151s, no sign of backlog), THEN deliberately at rpm=9 specifically to try to force backlog (avg_mt_latency actually LOWER at 0.109s, still no backlog). CONCLUSION: could not observe real backlog forming on this clip even under a deliberately constrained rpm=9 -- the flag has nothing to act on in either run (backlog_ratio stays ~0 throughout), so no live A/B differential is possible without a harder stress test. ROOT CAUSE (a 4th instance of the same underlying pattern this session): h-max-interim-duration-raise's fix (fewer, larger translation batches) also drastically cuts total translation-call FREQUENCY, which incidentally starves the backlog problem of its original trigger too -- the historical 41.5%-violation-rate run was recorded under the OLD 2.5s timer (many more, smaller, more frequent calls), not the now-validated 6.0s one. NOT rejecting the underlying idea -- the mechanism is implemented and verified correct -- but flagging that, like 3 other continuation/frequency-targeted hypotheses this session, its premise's original trigger condition (frequent small translation calls) has been substantially resolved by the timer fix already recommended for production. Would need either a much harder stress test (e.g. rpm=2-3, or a genuinely faster-spoken source) or a live run long/eventful enough to hit a real network/provider hiccup to observe this flag actually engaging.

hypotheses.title: Gate early soft-finalize on Deepgram's own per-word confidence, not just the fixed timer
hypotheses.description: h-max-interim-duration-raise (this session, live A/B) confirmed raising the fixed 2.5s soft-finalize timer to 6.0s cuts mid-utterance splits from 15/21 to 1/21 utterances and lowers max end-to-end latency ~29% -- but a fixed timer, longer or not, is still a blind proxy for 'has enough evidence arrived to commit'. x2streaming-asr2026 (found this session) frames streaming ASR as exactly this question (when to commit vs what to commit) and industry practice (found via a separate search) already gates partial-translation emission on ASR confidence exceeding ~0.7, retranslating only if the committed prefix later changes. This repo ALREADY logs a `confidence` field on every asr_interim event (deepgram_client.py's TranscriptionResult, confidence < 0.7 already flagged via the existing `is_low_confidence` property, currently only used to annotate displayed text with '[uncertain: ...]' in pipeline.py:393, not to gate commit timing) -- so this needs zero new API calls, just a new decision rule using data already flowing through the pipeline. Add an optional early-commit path: if a growing interim's confidence stays above a threshold (e.g. 0.85-0.9) for its own is_utterance_end-eligible span, allow a soft-finalize before the fixed max_interim_duration timer fires; if confidence drops, fall back to the existing timer/endpointing behavior unchanged.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: Should further reduce average commit latency beyond what h-max-interim-duration-raise alone achieves (committing confidently-correct speech sooner than a fixed 6s wait), without the cost or added round-trip of h-semantic-completeness-gating's extra LLM call, since it reuses data already collected. Risk: high ASR confidence does not equal semantically-complete (a confidently-transcribed word can still be mid-clause), so this may need to be combined with, not substituted for, a semantic check -- worth testing standalone first to isolate its own effect.
hypotheses.required_changes: New confidence-based early-commit branch in deepgram_client.py's soft-finalize path (same area as h-localagreement-asr-commit's _maybe_commit_local_agreement precedent), reading the already-populated `confidence` field, gated behind a new Config flag (e.g. ASR_CONFIDENCE_EARLY_COMMIT_THRESHOLD, None = disabled). Per PLAYBOOK.md's GENERATE_HYPOTHESES note, verify exactly which event kind(s) carry a populated `confidence` at the point this hook would read it (asr_interim per the grep in this entry's grounding, not assumed for other kinds) before implementing.
hypotheses.result_summary: Implemented (Config.asr_confidence_early_commit_threshold/_min_elapsed, wired through DeepgramTranscriber._force_finalize_loop's existing 0.5s periodic check -- see the implementation commit). Ran 2 live A/Bs against the h_max_interim_6s_test_v2 baseline (deepgram_max_interim_duration=6.0, rpm=60), varying only min_elapsed. PRE-CHECK finding that shaped both runs: this clip's confidence distribution is highly concentrated near 1.0 (91 asr_interim samples: median=0.999, p10=0.996, only a few outliers down to 0.82) -- confidence>=0.99 is satisfied almost immediately for nearly every interim on this clip. V1 (min_elapsed=3.0s): config diff confirmed clean (only the 2 new fields differ). RESULT: WORSE across the board, resembling LocalAgreement-2's failure mode. num_multi_batch_spans jumped from baseline's 1/21 to 11/14 (early-commit fired near the 3.0s floor almost every time, since confidence is essentially always satisfied), first_batch_duration_mean dropped 6.82s -> 3.93s (undoing most of h-max-interim-duration-raise's benefit). avg_mt_latency_seconds 0.177s -> 1.006s (~5.7x worse), avg_end_to_end +6%, max_end_to_end +14%. Coverage also collapsed: full_asr_len 1507 -> 863 chars (~43% less content processed in the same wall-clock window), full_translation_len 493 -> 315 chars -- the SAME coverage-collapse signature LocalAgreement-2 showed both times it was tested, now seen here too. Root cause: with confidence saturated near 1.0, the gate doesn't meaningfully discriminate -- it degenerates into 'soft-finalize every min_elapsed seconds regardless of confidence,' i.e. effectively just a much lower timer (3.0s instead of 6.0s), which is already known to be worse (this is exactly what h-max-interim-duration-raise showed by going the OTHER direction, 2.5s -> 6.0s). V2 (min_elapsed=5.0s, narrower window closer to the 6.0s ceiling): avoided v1's fragmentation and coverage collapse -- num_multi_batch_spans back to 1/21 (matching baseline's structure), full_asr_len 1507 -> 1594 (no coverage loss, if anything slightly more captured), cross-batch NE on the one remaining span actually improved (3.0 -> 0.83). But no clear latency win either: avg_end_to_end_latency_seconds +3.4% (6.182s -> 6.392s), max_end_to_end_latency_seconds +44% (6.589s -> 9.491s, a real outlier), avg_mt_latency +45% (0.177s -> 0.257s). Given the batching STRUCTURE is nearly identical to baseline (1 vs 1 multi-batch span), these latency differences are more plausibly live-run-to-run network/timing noise (documented before in this repo's own live-experiment caveats) than a genuine effect of the confidence gate itself, but this can't be fully disentangled with a single run per side. hypotheses.title: Repeated-sampling estimate of the compression instruction's guardrail-violation rate on segment 5

That result_summary explicitly flagged this as worth a smaller, targeted repeated-sampling follow-up rather than expanding the original hypothesis further, since n=1 cannot distinguish 'the model reliably violates this guardrail on this input' from 'a one-off sampling fluke'. This hypothesis reuses the exact same segment-5 source text (experiments/20260915_budget_translation_baseline.json, results.segments[5].asr) and calls LLMTranslator.translate_stream() directly N=10 times under compression_actions and N=10 times under the baseline_replay control (same model/dictionary/thinking_budget as the original replay, temperature/sampling otherwise default -- i.e. this measures the model's own run-to-run sampling variance, not a deliberate temperature sweep), scoring each output for whether it covers both clauses of the two-clause source ('course [...]' and 'you already know what's') via a cheap keyword/length heuristic (e.g. minimum expected character count and presence of a completion marker), with the fidelity judge run only on a small subsample (e.g. 3 of the 10 per condition) to keep Gemini spend low rather than judging all 20 outputs.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: If the segment-5 drop was a one-off sampling fluke, the compression_actions condition should complete the full two-clause translation in most (e.g. >=8/10) of the repeated samples, similar to baseline_replay's expected ~10/10. If it's a reliable behavior under this instruction (not just this one input), expect a materially higher truncation/drop rate under compression_actions than baseline_replay across the 10 repeats -- which would argue against shipping this instruction even opt-in without a stronger guardrail or a smaller, less ambiguous action set (e.g. dropping DROP/PARTIAL_SUMMARIZATION and keeping only PRONOMINALIZATION, which does not remove clauses).
hypotheses.required_changes: New script under src/real_time_translation/experiments/ (e.g. compression_repeated_sampling.py) that: (1) loads results.segments[5].asr from experiments/20260915_budget_translation_baseline.json (the exact source text that triggered the original drop), (2) calls LLMTranslator.translate_stream() with extra_system_instructions=COMPRESSION_INSTRUCTIONS (imported from compression_actions_replay.py, not re-typed) 10 times sequentially, and with extra_system_instructions=None 10 times sequentially as the paired control -- same model/dictionary/thinking_budget as the original replay run, (3) for each of the 20 outputs, records length and a simple heuristic completeness flag (does the translation contain content corresponding to both source clauses, checked by presence of translated-content markers for each clause rather than a strict regex, since exact Japanese wording varies run to run), (4) runs translation_fidelity_judge.judge() on 3 outputs per condition (chosen deterministically, e.g. the first 3) as a spot-check rather than all 20 to bound cost, (5) writes a normal experiments/YYYYMMDD_<name>.json with a per-sample table and a summary drop-rate-per-condition, plus a results.csv row.
hypotheses.result_summary:
Config-diff: by construction (single script, shared code path) the only variable between conditions is extra_system_instructions; both used the same model (gemini-3-flash-preview, thinking_budget=0), same dictionary, and the identical fixed context_lines=[seg2,seg3,seg4] with update_context=False for every one of the 20 calls, so no confound.

RESULT: the original n=1 segment-5 truncation is NOT a one-off sampling fluke -- it reproduces in 4/10 (40%) of compression_actions repeats (all four are byte-identical to the original run's 12-char truncated output 'ので、皆さんはすでに何が'), vs 0/10 truncations under baseline_replay (mean 34.7 chars, range 30-37, all cover both clauses). compression_actions output length is also far more variable (mean 22.4, range 12-30) than baseline (range 30-37). Fidelity-judge spot-check (3/10 samples per condition, to bound cost) caught the drop in only 1 of the 3 compression_actions samples checked (score 50, flagging 'course' and "already know what's" as dropped/ambiguous) and, notably, scored the two most-truncated 12-char outputs (repeats 0-1, in the spot-check sample) as 100 ('preserves the entirety of that fragment') -- because this script judges the single segment's source text against its translation in isolation, and segment 5's source is itself a fragment ("course. So I think you already know what's"), the judge has no way to know a continuation clause was expected. This means the char-length heuristic, not the narrowly-scoped judge, is the more reliable signal in THIS replay design -- a methodological limitation worth remembering for any future single-segment replay, not a property of the fidelity judge in general (the original n=1 run judged against the FULL multi-segment transcript, which is why it could meaningfully flag the drop).

IMPORTANT REFRAMING found while designing this script (not present in the original write-up): results.segments[4] and results.segments[5] in the source experiment have IDENTICAL source text (a duplicate/retry artifact of the recorded ASR stream, not two genuinely distinct utterances) and segment 4 is inside segment 5's own 3-line context window. Compressing/dropping content from segment 5 that was already fully said in segment 4 (its own immediate context) is arguably a CORRECT application of the instruction's own rule 9d ('omit a clause ONLY if it is pure repetition of something already fully conveyed earlier in <context>'), not a guardrail violation as h-compression-actions-prompt-instruction's result_summary originally framed it. This does not fully exonerate the instruction (the DROP still happened inconsistently -- 40% of the time, not reliably -- and a real production system would need duplicate-ASR-segment detection upstream to make this a safe, intentional behavior rather than a 40%-of-the-time coin flip), but it does mean the prior 'violates its own guardrail' framing is not established by this data -- it may instead be correctly detecting redundant ASR input. This specific 40% truncation rate is therefore NOT a general estimate of how often the compression instruction drops content on ordinary, non-duplicated segments -- testing that would need a different, non-duplicated multi-clause segment, flagged as a natural next follow-up rather than expanding this hypothesis further.

CONCLUSION: two things are now established that weren't before: (1) the original segment-5 behavior is reproducible (40% rate under identical resampling), so it is a real, non-negligible model behavior on this input, not noise; (2) the likely explanation is closer to 'the model sometimes (not reliably) applies its own DROP-on-repetition rule to a duplicated ASR segment' than 'the model violates an explicit anti-drop guardrail on genuinely new information' -- the latter framing is not supported once the segment-4/segment-5 duplication is accounted for. Net effect on h-compression-actions-prompt-instruction's own recommendation is unchanged (still not recommending production use as-is, now for a more precise reason: even a guardrail-compliant DROP that only fires 40% of the time on qualifying input is an unreliable, non-deterministic behavior a live captioning system should not depend on) -- but the root-cause story is now more accurate. $0.01 real API spend (20 short single-segment translate calls + 6 judge spot-check calls).

RESULT: zero content drops in either condition. baseline_replay: 10/10 repeats cover clause B (the 'function/image/label' clause), output_chars mean=93.0 (range 86-94). compression_actions: also 10/10 repeats cover clause B, output_chars mean=87.4 (range 85-97) -- about 6% shorter on average than baseline, consistent with mild SENTENCE_CUT/PARTIAL_SUMMARIZATION-style rewording rather than any DROP of clause content. Net effect on the parent hypothesis's recommendation: still not recommending shipping compression_actions into the production prompt as-is (a 6% length reduction is a modest benefit, and the segment-5 duplicate-input failure mode -- while now better understood -- is still an unreliable 40%-of-the-time behavior that would need explicit duplicate-ASR-segment detection upstream to be safe), but the specific 'unpredictable guardrail-violating content drop' concern is now understood as narrow (duplicate/redundant input specifically) rather than general. $0.01 real API spend (20 short single-segment translate calls + 6 judge spot-check calls).

hypotheses.title: Mechanically freeze the committed prefix on continuation batches, translate only the new source delta (API-compatible approximation of MT beam-search state reuse)
hypotheses.description: lacuna2026-beam-search-cascade-flicker (Rabatin/Seide/Chang, Interspeech 2024, added to papers.json this cycle) reports 20+% character flicker-rate reduction and +1 BLEU in a cascaded streaming ST system by reusing MT beam-search state across incremental ASR updates instead of retranslating from scratch -- directly targeting the same problem h-cross-utterance-flicker measured here (cross-batch translation NE ~1.47, i.e. near-total rewrite on continuation batches; see hypotheses.json). This repo's translator is API-based (Gemini/OpenAI via prompting, no beam-state access), so the paper's literal mechanism does not port -- but h-continuation-context-anchor already tried the natural prompting approximation (pass prior_translation as advisory <prior_translation> context, ask the model to preserve-or-extend) and got an inconclusive, noisy single-live-run result (cross-batch NE 0.836->0.972, flagged in its own result_summary as confounded by run-to-run translation-batch-boundary variance inherent to live runs). This hypothesis tests a STRUCTURALLY STRONGER approximation that lacuna2026's beam-state reuse actually guarantees but h-continuation-context-anchor's soft advisory instruction does not: mechanically freeze the already-committed translation text as a literal string prefix (no model involvement in reproducing it) and ask the model to translate ONLY the new source delta, then concatenate. This guarantees zero rewriting of the frozen portion by construction (matching what beam-search state reuse structurally guarantees), so the open question is not 'does NE drop' (it must, trivially, for the frozen portion) but whether the resulting Japanese reads naturally when a frozen earlier clause is followed by a freshly-translated later clause, and whether locking the prefix causes fidelity problems when an early batch's translation was wrong (e.g. from an ASR error later corrected) and can no longer be revised. Also fixes h-continuation-context-anchor's noisy-single-live-run methodological gap: since the per-batch English source deltas for multi-batch utterances are now recoverable from already-recorded experiment JSON (original_text is populated on translation_complete/translation_partial/asr_interim events for any experiment run since 2026-09-09 -- verified non-empty on experiments/20260915_h_continuation_anchor_test_rpmunlimited.json, 170/170 events), this can be tested as a deterministic, repeatable REPLAY over fixed recorded source deltas (same pattern as compression_actions_replay.py / compression_repeated_sampling*.py) with N repeats per condition per span, instead of one live run -- eliminating the live-run batching-variance confound entirely and allowing a real paired statistical comparison.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: Cross-batch translation NE for the hard-lock condition should be trivially near-zero for the frozen-prefix portion by construction (not itself informative), so the real signal to check is: (1) whether translation_fidelity_judge.py scores hard-lock outputs comparably to baseline/soft-anchor on the full reconstructed multi-batch utterance (checking for incoherent joins or stale/uncorrected errors carried in the frozen prefix), and (2) whether hard-lock's per-delta-batch chrF (against a matching reference sub-span) holds up despite the model never seeing/revising its own earlier output. If fidelity holds up, this is a stronger, structurally-guaranteed alternative to h-continuation-context-anchor's soft anchor; if fidelity drops (e.g. frozen early errors persist, or joins read unnaturally), that is itself a useful negative result bounding how far the beam-search-reuse analogy can be pushed under a pure prompting-API translator.
hypotheses.required_changes: New script src/real_time_translation/experiments/prefix_lock_replay.py, following compression_actions_replay.py's replay pattern (load an existing experiment JSON, drive LLMTranslator directly, zero new Deepgram spend): (1) reuse flicker_metrics.py's group_translation_by_utterance() to find multi-batch utterance spans in experiments/20260915_h_continuation_anchor_test_rpmunlimited.json (or another already-recorded multi-batch-rich JSON -- check which has the most multi-batch spans first); (2) for each span, extract per-batch original_text (English source delta) from translation_complete events in order; (3) for each span, run 3 conditions x N repeats (e.g. N=5): (a) baseline -- retranslate each batch's full accumulated source from scratch, matching current default behavior; (b) soft-anchor -- reproduce h-continuation-context-anchor's existing prior_translation advisory prompt path (llm_translator.py already supports this); (c) NEW hard-lock -- call LLMTranslator only on the NEW source delta text (not the full accumulated source) with the previous batches' emitted Japanese text passed as fixed prior context, then concatenate the frozen prior Japanese text + newly translated delta as the batch's output (no model call re-produces the frozen part). Needs a new LLMTranslator entry point or prompt mode for delta-only translation, OR can be approximated by calling the existing translate path with only the delta as source text and the frozen prefix in the context block -- check llm_translator.py's existing signature before deciding which is less invasive. (4) Compute cross-batch NE (reusing normalized_erasure()) and run translation_fidelity_judge.py against each span's full source text for a sample of repeats per condition. (5) Write experiments/YYYYMMDD_h_hard_prefix_lock_replay.json + results.csv row per this repo's logging convention.
hypotheses.result_summary:
Ran prefix_lock_replay.py (experiments/20260919_h_hard_prefix_lock_replay.json): deterministic replay of all 15 multi-batch utterance spans in experiments/20260915_h_continuation_anchor_test_rpmunlimited.json, x3 conditions (baseline_replay = retranslate cumulative source from scratch, today's default; soft_anchor_replay = h-continuation-context-anchor's existing advisory prior_translation; hard_lock = NEW, this hypothesis's mechanically-frozen-prefix + delta-only translation) x2 repeats each, same LLMTranslator instance/model (gemini-3-flash-preview) throughout so the only variable between conditions is the prompt strategy -- no config-diff confound risk the way a cross-machine live-run A/B has (see h-masking-holdback's rpm-limit near-miss).

CONFOUND CHECK (ANALYZE_RESULTS step): all 3 conditions ran in-process against the same translator instance with context_lines=[]/update_context=False for every call -- verified no model/thinking_budget/dictionary drift between conditions.

DATA-QUALITY FINDING (found this session, documented in the script's module docstring): TimedEvent.original_text on translation_complete events is NOT reliably cumulative across a multi-batch span -- checked across all 47 experiment JSONs, 1213/1591 (76%) of consecutive same-utterance batch transitions have the later batch's original_text prefixed by the earlier batch's, but 378/1591 (24%) show no overlap at all (i.e. original_text is sometimes the per-batch delta, sometimes the full accumulated source, inconsistently -- root cause not fully traced, plausibly async utterance_id bookkeeping in pipeline.py, not confirmed from a static read). Worked around by adaptively detecting prefix-containment per transition and rebuilding a self-consistent delta/cumulative source per batch rather than trusting the raw field's shape either way. Flagging as a new near-miss for PLAYBOOK.md's 'don't assume uniform field population' rule -- see reflections.md.

RESULTS -- mean cross-batch NE across the 15 spans: baseline_replay=0.597, soft_anchor_replay=0.212 (65% lower than baseline), hard_lock=0.0 in every single span/repeat (trivial by construction: the frozen portion literally cannot be rewritten, so this number alone is not informative about the technique's merit). hard_lock reached NE=0 in 15/15 spans; soft_anchor_replay reached NE=0 in 7/15; baseline_replay only 1/15. soft_anchor_replay's NE was <= baseline's in both repeats for 12/15 spans. Baseline also showed visibly higher REPEAT-TO-REPEAT variance in NE (e.g. span 13: 1.0 vs 1.586) than soft_anchor/hard_lock (mostly identical across repeats) -- anchoring (soft or hard) appears to reduce not just mean flicker but its run-to-run unpredictability too, a secondary finding worth a future hypothesis.

FIDELITY (translation_fidelity_judge.py, 1 repeat per span/condition, 45 judge calls total, English source vs each condition's final reconstructed span translation): mean score baseline_replay=99.3, soft_anchor_replay=98.7, hard_lock=90.7 (min 50, on 7/15 spans below 100). Manually inspected the worst case (span 3, source 'Until at the very end, the hope is that all of the | essential meaning of the passage', frozen prefix ends mid-clause right after 'the hope is that all of'): hard_lock's continuation restates '...という期待を持っており' (roughly 're-hoping that...') instead of grammatically completing the frozen clause, producing a redundant, less coherent Japanese sentence -- judge flagged 'Until' and 'the hope is that all of the essential meaning of the passage' as dropped/distorted (score 50), while baseline and soft_anchor both scored 100 on the same source. This is exactly the failure mode flagged as an open risk in this hypothesis's own predicted_effect.

CONCLUSION: hard_lock as implemented is NOT recommended -- its zero cross-batch NE is structurally guaranteed and therefore not a meaningful quality signal on its own, and it comes with a real, measurable fidelity cost concentrated in spans where the source sentence crosses a batch boundary mid-clause (a predictable, diagnosable failure mode, not random noise). The genuinely useful finding here is about soft_anchor_replay: under this controlled, repeated, deterministic replay methodology (fixing the exact live-run batching-variance confound h-continuation-context-anchor's own result_summary flagged as a limitation), the soft advisory prior_translation anchor gives a real, consistent, large reduction in cross-batch NE (0.597->0.212, and NE<=baseline in 12/15 spans) with negligible fidelity cost (99.3->98.7) -- the OPPOSITE conclusion from h-continuation-context-anchor's single noisy live run (which found NE getting slightly WORSE, 0.836->0.972, and explicitly flagged that as likely noise). RECOMMEND: treat h-continuation-context-anchor's live-run finding as superseded by this replay result for the specific question 'does the soft anchor reduce cross-batch NE' -- the anchor_continuation_translation flag looks like a real, low-risk win worth promoting out of experimental status, pending one more check (this replay used only spans from ONE clip/source file; a future hypothesis should re-run this same replay methodology against spans from other already-recorded multi-batch-rich experiment JSONs, e.g. experiments/20260915_llm_course_ep8_guest_talk_10min_rpm60.json which has 83 multi-batch spans, to check this generalizes beyond one clip). Per this repo's established precedent for replay/analysis-style experiments (e.g. compression_actions_replay.py), no results.csv row was added -- the output isn't a chrF/latency-comparable production run.

hypotheses.title: Does the soft-anchor cross-batch NE reduction generalize beyond one clip? Re-run the h-hard-prefix-lock-continuation replay methodology against a second, larger multi-batch-rich experiment JSON
hypotheses.description: h-hard-prefix-lock-continuation's replay (experiments/20260919_h_hard_prefix_lock_replay.json) found soft_anchor_replay gives a real, consistent cross-batch NE reduction (0.597->0.212 mean across 15 spans, NE<=baseline in 12/15 spans) with negligible fidelity cost (99.3->98.7), reversing h-continuation-context-anchor's own single noisy live-run finding (which saw NE get slightly worse). That result_summary explicitly flagged its own limitation: all 15 spans came from ONE source clip/experiment JSON (experiments/20260915_h_continuation_anchor_test_rpmunlimited.json), so the NE improvement could partly be a property of that clip's specific sentence structure rather than a general effect. This hypothesis re-runs the identical replay methodology (deterministic, repeated, in-process, same LLMTranslator instance across conditions -- no config-diff confound risk) against experiments/20260915_llm_course_ep8_guest_talk_10min_rpm60.json, which has 83 usable multi-batch spans (208 total batches) -- verified this cycle via _extract_spans(), roughly 5.5x the span count of the original replay -- to check whether the soft-anchor NE reduction holds up on a different, larger, differently-structured (guest interview vs the original clip's monologue) source.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: If the soft-anchor effect is a general property of anchoring continuation-batch retranslation to the utterance's own prior output (not an artifact of one clip), expect a similar direction and rough magnitude of cross-batch NE reduction for soft_anchor_replay vs baseline_replay on this second clip's 83 spans, with fidelity_judge scores staying close (small negative delta, not a collapse). A null or reversed result here would mean h-continuation-context-anchor's anchor_continuation_translation flag should NOT yet be promoted out of experimental status on the strength of the first replay alone. hard_lock is deliberately excluded from this run (already established as not recommended due to a real, diagnosed fidelity cost from mid-clause frozen-prefix joins) -- re-testing it here would not answer a new question and would roughly 1.5x the API spend for no new information.
hypotheses.required_changes: New script src/real_time_translation/experiments/soft_anchor_generalization_replay.py, adapted directly from prefix_lock_replay.py: same _extract_spans()/_translate_once()/_run_condition() logic, but (1) SOURCE_EXPERIMENT points at experiments/20260915_llm_course_ep8_guest_talk_10min_rpm60.json instead, (2) CONDITIONS reduced to ("baseline_replay", "soft_anchor_replay") only (drop hard_lock, already conclusively tested and not recommended), (3) OUT_JSON -> experiments/20260919_h_soft_anchor_generalization_guest_talk.json. Reuse flicker_metrics.normalized_erasure() and translation_fidelity_judge.judge() exactly as-is. No pipeline.py/llm_translator.py changes needed (prior_translation/delta_only params already exist from h-hard-prefix-lock-continuation).
hypotheses.result_summary:
Ran soft_anchor_generalization_replay.py (experiments/20260919_h_soft_anchor_generalization_guest_talk.json): identical replay methodology to h-hard-prefix-lock-continuation (same LLMTranslator instance for both conditions, context_lines=[]/update_context=False throughout), but against a second, much larger source: experiments/20260915_llm_course_ep8_guest_talk_10min_rpm60.json's 83 usable multi-batch spans (208 total batches), a guest-interview clip with visibly more disfluent/fragmentary ASR source text than the original clip (false starts, filler words, mid-sentence cuts).

CONFOUND CHECK: models config block is identical between this replay and its source experiment JSON (deepgram_model/llm_model/gemini_thinking_budget all match); single translator instance used for both conditions in-process, so no config drift between baseline_replay and soft_anchor_replay -- same no-confound guarantee as h-hard-prefix-lock-continuation. hard_lock intentionally excluded (already conclusively tested there, not recommended).

RESULTS -- mean cross-batch NE across the 83 spans: baseline_replay=0.630, soft_anchor_replay=0.107 (83% lower than baseline) -- a LARGER relative reduction than the original clip's 65% (0.597->0.212). soft_anchor_replay's per-span mean NE was <= baseline's in 81/83 spans (98%, vs 12/15=80% on the original clip). Of 166 individual repeat-runs, baseline hit NE=0 in only 9 (5%) vs soft_anchor's 123 (74%) -- consistent with the original clip's finding that anchoring reduces run-to-run flicker variance, not just its mean.

FIDELITY (translation_fidelity_judge.py, 1 repeat per span/condition, 166 judge calls total): mean score baseline_replay=92.95, soft_anchor_replay=89.04 (-3.9 points). This drop is larger in absolute terms than the original clip's (-0.6, 99.3->98.7), and this clip's BASELINE fidelity itself is already notably lower (92.95 vs 99.3) -- plausibly because this clip's source is intrinsically harder to translate cleanly (disfluent spoken interview vs the original's more monologue-like structure), which may also amplify any anchoring-side hallucination risk. Manually inspected the single worst case (span 69, judge score 0): source 'our paper, we just like a like like a AIM to' (a genuinely fragmentary, cut-off utterance). baseline's from-scratch retranslation of the fuller context produced a generic, non-committal continuation ('目指しているのは、その' -- 'what we're aiming for is...'), while soft_anchor's advisory-anchored continuation invented a specific but unsupported acronym expansion ('AIMEを目標としているかのようで' -- 'as if aiming for AIME'), a hallucination not present in the ambiguous source. This is a new failure mode distinct from h-hard-prefix-lock-continuation's mid-clause-split issue: soft-anchoring's continuation instinct can fabricate content to make an ambiguous/cut-off fragment cohere with its own prior translation, rather than staying agnostically vague like a from-scratch retranslation does. It appeared to affect a minority of spans (16/83 scored <80 under soft_anchor vs 10/83 under baseline) concentrated in spans with visibly disfluent/fragmentary source text (see the top-5 worst-delta spans, e.g. span 7 'based on the we will give you oh,', span 29 'future to pro promoting to let the answer some questions.').

CONCLUSION: the core finding GENERALIZES -- soft_anchor_replay's cross-batch NE reduction is not an artifact of the original clip; if anything it is stronger on this second, larger, structurally different clip (83% vs 65% relative reduction, 98% vs 80% of spans improved-or-equal). The fidelity trade-off is real and clip-dependent: negligible on cleaner source (original clip, -0.6) but more noticeable on disfluent/fragmentary source (this clip, -3.9), with a specific, diagnosable hallucination pattern (inventing content to cohere with the anchor rather than staying vague) concentrated in the messiest utterances. RECOMMEND: the anchor_continuation_translation flag still looks like a good default given the NE win generalizes and is large, but flag the hallucination-under-disfluency failure mode explicitly if/when promoting it out of experimental status -- a future hypothesis could test whether gating the anchor off (falling back to from-scratch retranslation) specifically for very short/fragmentary source deltas mitigates this without losing the NE win on cleaner speech. Per established precedent for replay/analysis-style experiments, no results.csv row added (not a chrF/latency-comparable production run).

hypotheses.title: Gate the soft-anchor continuation prompt off for very short/fragmentary source deltas to avoid the hallucination-under-disfluency failure mode while keeping the cross-batch NE win
hypotheses.description: h-soft-anchor-generalization-guest-talk confirmed soft_anchor_replay's cross-batch NE reduction generalizes (83% relative reduction on 83 guest-talk spans, even larger than the original clip's 65%), but also found the fidelity cost is clip-dependent and concentrated in disfluent/fragmentary source: mean fidelity dropped -3.9 points on the guest-talk clip vs -0.6 on the cleaner original clip, and manual inspection of the worst case (span 69, delta_text 'our paper, we just like a like like a AIM to') showed the anchor's continuation instinct fabricating a specific but unsupported acronym expansion ('AIME') to make an ambiguous, cut-off fragment cohere with its own prior translation -- a hallucination the from-scratch baseline did not produce (it stayed vague instead). That result_summary explicitly proposed gating the anchor off for very short/fragmentary deltas as the next concrete follow-up. This hypothesis implements and tests the simplest such gate: a per-batch word-count threshold on delta_text (the NEW source fragment for that batch, not the cumulative text) -- below the threshold, fall back to baseline (prior_translation=None, from-scratch retranslation of the cumulative text); at or above it, use the existing soft-anchor path unchanged. Tests on both already-replayed source experiments (the original 15-span clip and the 83-span guest-talk clip) to check the gate preserves the NE win on the clip where it was clean (minimal regression expected, few/no deltas are short there) while reducing or eliminating the fidelity drop on the guest-talk clip's short-delta spans (where the failure mode was concentrated).
hypotheses.predicted_effect: For spans whose short/fragmentary batches get gated to baseline: expect those specific batches' fidelity to move back toward baseline's (higher than pure soft-anchor), at the cost of losing some of the NE reduction on exactly those batches (baseline rewrites more). Averaged across all spans, expect gated_soft_anchor to land between baseline_replay and soft_anchor_replay on both metrics -- NE noticeably lower than baseline (most batches are not short, so most of the win is retained) and mean fidelity closer to baseline than pure soft-anchor is, with the specific span-69-style hallucination (inventing content to cohere with an ambiguous cut-off fragment) reduced or gone on gated batches. A null result (gating barely changes either metric) would mean the threshold picked is wrong (too low to catch the failure cases, or too high and gating too much) or that delta_text word count is not actually a good proxy for 'fragmentary/ambiguous' -- worth checking against the specific short-delta spans flagged in the guest-talk result before concluding either way.
hypotheses.required_changes: New script src/real_time_translation/experiments/soft_anchor_disfluency_gate_replay.py, adapted from soft_anchor_generalization_replay.py / prefix_lock_replay.py: reuse _extract_spans() and _translate_once() unchanged. Add a new _run_condition-equivalent path for 'gated_soft_anchor' that mirrors the existing soft_anchor_replay loop in prefix_lock_replay.py's _run_condition() but checks len(batch.delta_text.split()) < GATE_MIN_WORDS (start with GATE_MIN_WORDS=5 as a first cut, chosen because span 69's flagged delta_text has 9 words but is still a cut-off fragment ending mid-clause -- note in result_summary if 5 turns out too high/low based on which spans actually get gated vs which ones still show the failure mode) for each batch i>0; if gated, call with prior_translation=None (same as baseline for that one batch) but still update prev_full_output from the OUTPUT so a later, longer batch in the same span can still anchor off it. Run against BOTH already-recorded source experiments already used by the two prior hypotheses in this line (experiments/20260915_h_continuation_anchor_test_rpmunlimited.json, 15 spans, and experiments/20260915_llm_course_ep8_guest_talk_10min_rpm60.json, 83 spans) with CONDITIONS=(baseline_replay, soft_anchor_replay, gated_soft_anchor) -- hard_lock stays excluded, already settled. Reuse flicker_metrics.normalized_erasure() and translation_fidelity_judge.judge() as-is. Also record, per span, which batch indices were gated (delta word count below threshold) so the report can point at the specific gated spans/batches when checking whether the targeted failure mode actually improved there.
hypotheses.result_summary: Config check: both source experiments used identical models (gemini-3-flash-preview, thinking_budget=0) -- no confound. Mixed/partial result. NE landed strictly between baseline and soft_anchor on both clips as predicted (original clip: baseline 0.613, gated 0.408, soft 0.233; guest-talk: baseline 0.622, gated 0.547, soft 0.123), but GATE_MIN_WORDS=5 gated a much larger share of eligible (i>0) batches than expected -- 40% (8/20) on the clean original clip and 57% (71/125) on the guest-talk clip, contradicting the predicted 'most batches are not short' assumption -- so on the guest-talk clip the gate retained only ~12% relative NE reduction vs soft_anchor's 80%, i.e. it fell back toward baseline's flicker for the majority of batches. The exact flagged failure case (span 69, the 'AIME' hallucination) WAS fixed as intended: judge score 50 (soft_anchor) -> 100 (gated), matching baseline. But the AGGREGATE fidelity numbers (guest-talk: baseline 92.71, gated 90.67, soft 88.41; original: baseline 98.67, soft 98.33, gated 96.67 -- gated even below both here) are not reliable: judge() is only called once per condition per span (on repeats[0]), and a noise-floor check on spans where the gate had literally zero code-path effect (no batch gated, so gated_soft_anchor==soft_anchor_replay by construction, differences are pure LLM sampling variance) shows swings of -30..+5 (original clip, n=7) and -5..+45 (guest-talk, n=13) -- comparable to or larger than the gated-spans mean effect (0.00 n=8 and +1.84 n=68 respectively). The aggregate fidelity signal cannot be distinguished from single-sample judge noise at this scale. Conclusion: the gating MECHANISM works for the specific hallucination pattern it targeted, but GATE_MIN_WORDS=5 is calibrated too high for disfluent interview speech (gates away most of the NE win) and the current judge-on-repeats[0]-only design cannot confirm a net fidelity benefit. Not abandoning -- recommend a follow-up with a lower threshold (2-3 words) and judge() called on every repeat (not just repeats[0]) to get a real noise estimate per span, focused on the specific spans that were actually gated rather than the whole-span aggregate.

hypotheses.title: Recalibrate GATE_MIN_WORDS using an actual delta_text word-count histogram, and call judge() on every repeat instead of just repeats[0], to get a trustworthy fidelity signal
hypotheses.description: h-soft-anchor-disfluency-gate (cycle 19) found two concrete calibration problems, both flagged in its own result_summary as the recommended follow-up: (1) GATE_MIN_WORDS=5 gated far more batches than predicted (40% on the clean original clip, 57% on the guest-talk clip), because the threshold was picked from a single quoted example rather than the actual delta_text word-count distribution, and (2) the aggregate fidelity comparison used judge() only once per condition per span (repeats[0]), and a same-code-path noise check (spans where gating had zero effect) showed judge-score swings of -30..+5 and -5..+45 -- as large as or larger than the reported mean effects -- so the aggregate fidelity numbers could not be trusted. This hypothesis fixes both, per the process improvement written into reflections.md cycle 19: before picking a numeric threshold on an already-recorded field, compute its actual distribution first. Done during this hypothesis's own design (see note below) rather than left to the experiment: a word-count histogram over both source experiments' i>0 batches (145 eligible batches total) shows median delta_text length is only 4-5 words in both clips, so GATE_MIN_WORDS=5 was gating at-or-above the median, not just outlier fragments. At GATE_MIN_WORDS=2, gating drops to 10% (2/20) on the original clip and 16% (20/125) on the guest-talk clip -- a much more targeted gate. Critically, re-checking the specific failure case this line of hypotheses targets (guest-talk span 69) against the actual recorded per-batch data (not the quoted description) shows the batch that produced the 'AIME' hallucination has delta_text 'AIM to' (2 words, batch index 1), not the 9-word string quoted in h-soft-anchor-disfluency-gate's description (that 9-word string was batch 0's delta, a different batch) -- so GATE_MIN_WORDS=2 still catches the actual target failure case, while gating far fewer batches overall than 5 did.
hypotheses.predicted_effect: With GATE_MIN_WORDS=2: expect gated_soft_anchor's mean NE to sit much closer to soft_anchor_replay's (less falling back to baseline-like flicker) than the GATE_MIN_WORDS=5 run did, since far fewer batches are gated (10%/16% vs 40%/57% of eligible batches). With judge() called on every repeat (not just repeats[0]): expect a per-span noise estimate (stdev or range across repeats, same condition) directly measured rather than inferred post-hoc from zero-effect spans, and expect the gated-vs-soft_anchor fidelity difference on the guest-talk clip's actually-gated spans (including span 69) to be tested against that measured noise floor rather than reported as a bare mean difference. A null/mixed result here would mean either the word-count gate is fundamentally too coarse a proxy for 'ambiguous/fragmentary' even at 2 words (worth comparing against which gated batches still show hallucination-style errors), or that per-span fidelity noise is large enough that no threshold choice can be validated with REPEATS=2-3 judge calls -- both are informative negative results, not failures of the experiment.
hypotheses.required_changes: Adapt src/real_time_translation/experiments/soft_anchor_disfluency_gate_replay.py (or a new soft_anchor_gate_recalibrated_replay.py importing its _run_gated_condition, unchanged except GATE_MIN_WORDS): (1) set GATE_MIN_WORDS=2 (from the histogram computed during this hypothesis's design, see description); (2) change the judge_scores block to call judge(source_full, translation_full) once per repeat per condition (iterate condition_repeats[condition], not just repeats[0]) and store a list of scores per condition per span instead of a single score, so mean/stdev across repeats can be computed directly; keep REPEATS=2 (do not increase -- this doubles judge() calls which are the dominant cost driver, not the translate calls). Run against the same two already-recorded source experiments (experiments/20260915_h_continuation_anchor_test_rpmunlimited.json, experiments/20260915_llm_course_ep8_guest_talk_10min_rpm60.json). In ANALYZE_RESULTS, explicitly report the per-span judge-score spread for gated_soft_anchor vs soft_anchor_replay on spans that were actually gated (including span 69) and compare the gated-vs-ungated mean difference against that spread, not just an aggregate mean, per the noise-floor check already added to PLAYBOOK.md's ANALYZE_RESULTS section in cycle 19.
hypotheses.result_summary: Config check: both source experiments used identical models (gemini-3-flash-preview, thinking_budget=0) -- no confound. Mixed result, and a design flaw discovered in this hypothesis's own gating logic. NE (flicker): GATE_MIN_WORDS=2 gated far fewer eligible batches than MIN_WORDS=5 did, as predicted by the word-count histogram (original clip: 2/20 = 10% vs cycle19's 8/20 = 40%; guest-talk: 20/125 = 16% vs cycle19's 71/125 = 57%), and NE landed much closer to soft_anchor_replay on the guest-talk clip as a result (baseline 0.649, gated 0.307, soft 0.123 -- vs cycle19's gated=0.547, a big flicker improvement from the recalibration) and stayed similar on the original clip (baseline 0.665, gated 0.290, soft 0.232). Fidelity: this run finally computed a real per-span noise floor by calling judge() on every repeat instead of just repeats[0] (not just inferring it post-hoc from zero-effect spans as cycle19 did). Result: the noise floor is even larger than cycle19's post-hoc estimate suggested -- stdev 3.23 (original clip, n=52 same-code-path resamples) and stdev 17.72 (guest-talk, n=251) -- while the actual gated-vs-soft_anchor mean fidelity difference on batches that were actually gated is 0.0 (original, 2 gated spans) and 4.0 (guest-talk, 20 gated spans, individual diffs -5..+50). Both are far inside their respective noise floors, so the net fidelity benefit of gating remains NOT confirmed, exactly as it was at MIN_WORDS=5 -- recalibrating the threshold fixed the NE side but did not (and structurally cannot, at REPEATS=2 judge-call scale) resolve the fidelity question. DESIGN FLAW found during analysis (not caught at design time): this hypothesis's own description claimed GATE_MIN_WORDS=2 'still catches the actual target failure case' (guest-talk span 69, batch index 1, delta_text 'AIM to', 2 words) -- but the gating condition in soft_anchor_disfluency_gate_replay.py is `len(delta_text.split()) < GATE_MIN_WORDS` (strict less-than), so a 2-word delta is NOT gated when GATE_MIN_WORDS=2 (2 < 2 is False). Confirmed in this run's own output JSON: span 69's gated_batch_indices is [], i.e. the flagship hallucination case this whole line of hypotheses was designed around was silently NOT exercised by the gate at all in this run, on either condition. The 'AIME' mistranslation still happened to get corrected in the gated_soft_anchor condition for span 69 this run, but that must be attributed to LLM sampling variance on the ungated soft-anchor path, not to the gate -- a coincidence, not the mechanism working. Root cause: nobody verified the boundary condition (delta_text word count == GATE_MIN_WORDS) against the actual comparison operator before writing the hypothesis description. Conclusion: not abandoning the general gating idea (the NE improvement from recalibration is real and clearly followed the histogram's prediction), but the specific claim of 'still catches span 69' was wrong, and the fidelity benefit is still statistically unconfirmed even with a proper noise floor now measured. Recommend GATE_MIN_WORDS=3 (uses <=, catches 2-word deltas without over-gating) as a follow-up if this line is pursued further, and recommend against trusting single-repeat judge() fidelity numbers anywhere else in this codebase without the same noise-floor check, given how large the measured stdevs turned out to be (17.7 points on the guest-talk clip).

hypotheses.result_summary: Config diff against cycle 20's noisefloor-replay JSON confirmed gate_min_words is the ONLY difference (deepgram_model/llm_provider/llm_model/gemini_thinking_budget/repeats_per_condition all identical) -- no confound. The arithmetic fix is CONFIRMED directly in this run's own output: guest-talk span 69 batch 1 ('AIM to', 2 words) has span_69_batch1_gated=True this time (2 < 3 is True), vs. cycle 20's gated_batch_indices=[] for that span (2 < 2 was False). Gating rates landed within the predicted band: 25% (5/20) on the original clip and 34% (42/125) on guest-talk, between threshold=2's 10%/16% and threshold=5's 40%/57%. Fidelity: gated_soft_anchor vs soft_anchor_replay mean diff on gated spans is +2.0 (original clip, n=40 noise-floor scores, noise_floor_stdev=4.32) and +3.51 (guest-talk, n=163, noise_floor_stdev=14.54) -- both diffs are well inside their own noise floor, so INCONCLUSIVE for fidelity, consistent with cycle 20's and h-judge-noise-repeats-power-check's finding that REPEATS=2 judge() calls cannot resolve fidelity effects of this size in this codebase, independent of which GATE_MIN_WORDS value is used (now a third consistent data point). But on the guest-talk clip, where gating fires much more (42/125), gated_soft_anchor's mean_ne (0.377) is markedly WORSE (more flicker) than soft_anchor_replay's (0.089) -- the opposite of the intended direction; both remain much better than the ungated baseline_replay's 0.626.
